analytic.title: An Effective Approach for Improving Responsiveness of Total Bandwidth Server

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: As a result of increasing in diversity and complexity, real-time embedded systems have to deal with both periodic and aperiodic tasks. In such systems, it is expected that response time of aperiodic tasks is as short as possible. Total Bandwidth Server (TBS) is one of effective task scheduling algorithms for a mixture of periodic and aperiodic tasks. As a successor to TBS, Adaptive TBS (ATBS) is an algorithm where TBS is enhanced with prediction of execution times. Virtual release advancing (VRA) is an additional technique for TBS to shorten response time of tasks and Enhanced VRA (EVRA) is the extended version of VRA with lightweight complexity. In this paper, combination of ATBS and EVRA is examined to further improve the responsiveness of TBS. Simulation results show that the combination can reduce response times by up to 25% compared with TBS under heavy loads, while maintaining the schedulability and relatively low time complexity of the system.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time embedded systems are increasing in diversity and complexity, where many different types of tasks including periodic and aperiodic ones are involved in a system. Therefore, task scheduling algorithms for both periodic and aperiodic tasks are now required. Total Bandwidth Server (TBS) [1] is known as one of persuasive scheduling algorithms.

In many real-time embedded systems, it is expected that aperiodic tasks finish in short response times. In order to satisfy this demand, adaptive TBS (ATBS) was introduced in [2]. ATBS suggests using predictive execution times rather than worst-case execution times in deadline calculation, so that earlier absolute deadlines are obtained for the target aperiodic tasks. This method reduces response times of aperiodic tasks by up to 39% under heavy loads [2].

Virtual release advancing (VRA) [3], [4] is another approach to improve the responsiveness in the context of TBS. VRA tries to use virtual release (arrival) times instead of actual release times in deadline calculation. Simulation results of TBS combined with VRA showed improvement by 15% in responsiveness.
An enhanced version of VRA (EVRA) was successively proposed to mitigate a problem of hight time complexity in VRA [5].

In this paper, combination of ATBS and EVRA is investigated. The combinational method is expected to further reduce response times with relatively low time complexity while guaranteeing the schedulability of the system.

The rest of this paper is composed as follows: Related work including ATBS and (E)VRA algorithms is presented in Section II. Section III describes the proposed method in details. The method is then evaluated in Section IV. Finally, the paper concludes in Section V.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: The method proposed in this paper exploits both ATBS and (E)VRA for further shortening response times. These techniques are first reviewed as prior work in this section.
These techniques are developed in the context of TBS which serves aperiodic tasks. In the TBS, the following formula 1 is employed to calculate tasks' absolute deadlines.
div.formula: d k = max(r k , d k-1 ) + C k U s(1)
div.p: In this formula, k means the kth aperiodic task and d k , r k , and C k are the absolute deadline, release (arrival) time, and worst-case execution time of the kth aperiodic task, respectively. The calculated d k-1 is the absolute deadline of the k-1th (previous) task. Finally, U s is the bandwidth of the server, that is, a processor utilization factor by aperiodic tasks which are served by TBS. After assigning absolute deadlines, aperiodic tasks are inserted into the system and scheduled based on the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) algorithm [6].

Originating from the formula 1, the prior works have their own approach to obtain earlier deadlines for the target tasks. While ATBS focuses on shortening the C k term by predicting execution times, (E)VRA pays attention to retroactively advancing the release time with virtual release times.

In the original TBS, worst-case execution times (WECTs), which in most cases are pessimistically estimated larger than the actual execution times, are used for deadline calculations. These WCETs prevent tasks from being scheduled preferentially under EDF-based scheduling algorithms. Therefore, estimation with shorter C k is desirable for obtaining shorter deadlines. ATBS is to satisfy this preference by introducing predictive execution times (PETs) which are shorter than WCETs. Figure 1 illustrates an example of scheduling by ATBS. In the figure, there are two periodic tasks and one aperiodic task. The first periodic task, τ 1 , has the period of T 1 = 3 and execution time of C 1 = 1. The second one, τ 2 , has T 2 = 8 and C 2 = 2. The processor utilization by these periodic tasks is then U p = 1/3 + 2/8 = 7/12, which leads to the processor utilization reserved for the aperiodic task (or the server) being U s = 1 -U p = 5/12. The aperiodic task is assumed to enter the system at t = 2 with its WCET of 5. In this situation, according to the formula 1 for the original TBS, the aperiodic task is assigned an absolute deadline of d k = 14. This task is scheduled to start at t = 4 and then finishes at t = 5 if the actual execution time of the aperiodic task is one, which results in the response time of three.

On the other hand, when ATBS with a PET of two for this task is applied, the aperiodic task is given a deadlines of d P ET = 7, seven slots earlier than the original TBS. With this earlier deadline, the target task can preempt the first instance of τ 2 and start immediately at t = 2. (The red instance in the Figure 1.) As a result, the target task finishes at t = 3 with two-slot shorter response time.

In the other approach, (E)VRA introduces virtual release times (vr k ) earlier than the actual release times (r k ). In the formula 1, r k is replaced by vr k in order to obtain an earlier deadline for the target task. Figure 2, for instance, shows a schedule by (E)VRA with two periodic tasks, τ 1 and τ 2 , and an aperiodic task. τ 1 has a period of T 1 = 2 and execution time of C 1 = 1 and τ 2 has T 2 = 3 and C 2 = 1. The processor utilization by the periodic tasks is U p = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6 and the bandwidth of the server is U s = 1 -5/6 = 1/6. The aperiodic task is released at t = 9 with its execution time of one. The absolute deadline which the original TBS assigns to this aperiodic task is d k = 15. Then this task is scheduled at t = 11 and finishes at t = 12 with the response time of three.

By applying (E)VRA, an earlier virtual release time for this target task is supposed to be at t = 6 and therefore a (virtual) deadline is calculated at vd k = 12 which is equal to the deadline for the fourth instance of τ 2 . With the assumption that ties break in favor of aperiodic tasks, As a result, the target task is scheduled at t = 9 and finishes at t = 10, giving the response time of one.

div.head: III. PROPOSED METHOD
div.p: Now that we have reviewed the two techniques, we try to combine them for further improving response times. Since the two techniques are independent of each other, the combination can be done straightforward, that is, shorter predictive execution times and earlier virtual release times are supposed at the same time. Before forming the proposed algorithm, let us take a look at the following example which clarifies the feasibility of the combination.

div.head: A. Example of the proposed method
div.p: An example of the proposed method is shown in Figure 3 According to the original TBS, an absolute deadline is calculated for the aperiodic task at d k = 16. Therefore, the target aperiodic task is scheduled at t = 6 and its response time is two. With (E)VRA, as depicted in Figure 3 (1), an earlier virtual release time, vr k = 3, is supposed for the target task. Then, the target task is given the virtual deadline vd k = 15, one slot earlier than the original deadline. This earlier deadline is still later than that of the second instance of τ 2 . Thus, there is no effect to the schedule of the target task.

In another case of ATBS (Figure 3(2)), the predictive execution time is assumed to be two. Substituting this predictive execution time into Formula 1, ATBS assigns an absolute deadline of d P ET = 9 for the target task. Although it is sevenslot earlier than the original one, this deadline cannot help schedule the target task earlier than the second instance of τ 2 . Now, by concurrently using the predictive execution time of two and the virtual release time of t = 3 in the formula 1, the virtual and predictive deadline (vd P ET ) is calculated at t = 8 as shown in Figure 3 (3). This deadline is equal to that for the second instance of τ 2 . In favor of aperiodic tasks, the target task is immediately scheduled at t = 4 ahead of the instance of τ 2 and finishes at t = 5 with the response time of one. This example indicates that the combinational method has more chances of shortening response times than either TBS or (E)VRA.

div.head: B. Definition of the proposed method
div.p: As a combinational algorithm, the proposed method is composed of two phases with respect to execution time prediction and tentative deadline calculation.

1) Execution time prediction: According to the literature for ATBS [2], execution time is predicted by referring to the past execution times of a task1 . Formula 2 shows the calculation of a predictive execution time (PET).
div.formula: C P ET k = α * C P ET k-1 + (1 -α) * C AET k-1 (2
div.p: C P ET k means PET for the kth (current) instance of the target task. C P ET k-1 and C AET k-1 are PET and actual execution time (AET) of the previous instance of the task, respectively. The initial value of PET, C P ET0 , is equal to WCET of the task. α is a weighting coefficient (0 ≤ α ≤ 1). By using this formula, calculated PETs are in most cases shorter than WCETs.

div.head: 2) Tentative deadline calculation:
div.p: The second phase is to calculate a tentative deadline for the target task. When an aperiodic task is released, it is assigned an absolute deadline calculated by Formula 3 using C P ET k obtained in the first phase and virtual release time (vr k ) designated by the (E)VRA algorithm.
div.formula: d P ET k = max(vr k , d k-1 ) + C P ET k U s (3)
div.p: Since PET might be shorter than the real execution time in some cases, the target task might not finish within the PET. In such cases of underestimation, the absolute deadline is recalculated when the PET expires, so that the target task is rescheduled with the updated deadline. In order to update the absolute deadline, Formula 4 is employed.
div.formula: d UP D k = d P ET k + C W CET -C P ET k U s (4)
div.p: In this recalculation, the remaining execution time is regarded as REST = C W CET -C P ET k . In fact, there can be various options to define the remaining execution time, such as random, mean point, or applying the incremental deadline update method presented in the literature [7].
These methods, however, might cause additional overheads of repeated deadline calculation. We choose the above recalculation with REST since it limits the recalculation to only once.

div.head: C. Procedures of the proposed algorithm
div.p: In this section, the detailed procedures of the combinational algorithm are described.

Algorithm 1 shows the procedures for predicting the execution time and calculating a tentative absolute deadline for the kth instance of a given aperiodic task. In the first phase from line 1 to line 4, PET for the kth instance is calculated as C P ET k by using Formula 2. Here, the weighting coefficient α is supposed to be 0.5. The (k -1)th (previous) PET (C P ET k-1 ) and AET (C AET k-1 ) are values recorded by the operating system. The second phase from line 5 and line 16 runs the EVRA algorithm to determine and assign an absolute deadline to the kth instance. vd k is the virtual deadline for the instance and initialized at line 6 with the actual release time r k and the obtained predictive execution time C P ET k . According to the EVRA algorithm, vd k , vd , and vd are prepared as limits of advancing for the previous deadline, the last empty slot, and the last starting time of τ max , respectively. For preparation,the operating system keeps observing the systematical parameters: the previous deadline (d k-1 ), the last empty slot number (last empty), and the starting time of the last instance of the task which has the longest period (ls max ). The details for these limits are found in [5]. The limit of the previous deadline is first examined in lines 10 to 13. If the release time is earlier than or equal to the previous deadline, the virtual deadline is then set to the corresponding limit and the algorithm closes. Otherwise, there is a possibility of advancing the release time and correspondingly the deadline. The algorithm starts the advancing loop (Advancing Loop) at line 15 with the maximum value among the three limits as a bound.
div.formula: C P ET k = α * C P ET k-1 + (1 -α) * C AET k-1 ; 5: /*
div.p: Advancing Loop is a function for tracking the past schedule backward and obtaining a possibly earliest absolute deadline as an output vd k . The tracking is done on a past-instance basis using an input tracking array S[] which is recorded by the operating system to keep the starting time of the previously executed instances. The codes for Advancing Loop is shown in Algorithm 2.

Algorithm 2: Advancing Loop The use of ATBS involves a possibility of underestimating PETs and the the actual execution might exceed the PET. In such cases, the target task's deadline has to be updated. This is done by a procedure shown in Algorithm 3, which is called every tick timing. The update procedure begins with checking the occurrence of underestimation at line 2, where the remaining PET (C RP ET k ) reaches zero but the task is not finished. (It is supposed that the remaining PET is decreased every tick timing.) If this condition is satisfied, it means the underestimation occurs and the absolute deadline is updated at line 3, where the remaining execution time is regarded as wcet -C P ET k .

div.head: A. Simulation methodology
div.p: The proposed method is evaluated by simulation with synthetic task sets. The target criteria are response times and additional runtime overhead. There are totally 80 sets of periodic tasks with the processor utilization (U p ) of 60% to 95% at an interval of 5%. In addition, we prepared several sets of aperiodic tasks of which processor utilization is about 2% in the observation period of 100,000 ticks. The servers capacity is set to U s = 1 -U p . Related periods and WCETs are generated by exponential distributions.
The following seven methods are compared. 1) Original TBS (TBS) 2) Original TBS with virtual release advancing (TBS+VRA)

3) Original TBS with enhanced virtual release advancing (TBS+EVRA) 4) Adaptive TBS (ATBS) 5) Adaptive TBS with virtual release advancing (ATBS+VRA) 6) Adaptive TBS with enhanced virtual release advancing (ATBS+EVRA) 7) Constant Bandwidth Server (CBS) [8] A resource reclaiming technique described in the literature [9] is applied to all the methods above except CBS.

div.head: B. Response time
div.p: Figure 4 shows results of average response times in ticks. Since EVRA inherently has the same effects for responsiveness as VRA, the two methods give equivalent results and therefore they are depicted by the same lines (TBS+VRA/EVRA and ATBS+VRA/EVRA). As shown in the figure, the proposed method (ATBS+VRA/EVRA) gives the best results in reducing the response times. This achievement indicates that the combinational method benefits from the advantages of both ATBS and (E)VRA in terms of shortening deadlines. Furthermore,when the periodical utilization is increasing, the number of empty slots obviously decreases. Since empty slot is one of the limits of the (E)VRA technique, the less empty slots exist, the more backward to the past the virtual release times are advanced and then the much earlier the deadlines are calculated. On the other words, the proposed method is highly effective on responsiveness at heavy loads. Especially, under heavy loads of 95%, the proposed method is effective in reducing the response time by 8% compared to ATBS, 19% to TBS+(E)VRA, and to the original TBS.

div.head: C. Runtime overhead
div.p: The runtime overhead is assessed according to the maximum additional runtime per tick. The number of cycles taken to execute each scheduling algorithm is concerned to compute the runtime overheads. We suppose each scheduler is implemented with Cortex-A9 instructions and take into account the required execution cycles for each instruction (arithmetic, logical, and control operations) [10], [11].

Results of maximum additional runtime overhead per tick are exhibited in Figure 5. As shown in the figure, TBS, ATBS, and CBS have negligible runtime overheads. On the other hand, it is confirmed that EVRA brings much reduction in runtime overhead compared with VRA (TBS+VRA vs. TBS+EVRA or ATBS+VRA vs. ATBS+EVRA). ATBS+EVRA has relatively low time complexity, while ATBS+VRA involves the worst overhead. Certainly, ATBS+EVRA successfully decreases the overhead by up to 60% compared with the ATBS+VRA under U p of 95%. Furthermore, ATBS+EVRA even show lower runtime overhead than TBS+EVRA since the earlier deadlines calculate by ATBS contribute to the earlier completion of release advancing.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, with the aim of further improving the responsiveness of TBS-based scheduling, a combinational method of ATBS and EVRA is proposed. In the evaluation by simulations, this combination helped to reduce the average response times by up to 25% compared to the original TBS. In addition, combination of ATBS and EVRA showed reduction in the runtime overhead by up to 60% compared with that of ATBS and VRA.

In this study, the evaluation was done by simulations with synthetic task sets. In the future, it should be considered to implement and evaluate the proposed method in actual real-time systems, where more exact information on runtime overheads can be obtained.
Furthermore, applying the proposed method to scheduling on multiprocessor systems is a considerable research interest.
